title: Each Person Answers for Themselves
overview: Speaking to exiles who blamed their suffering on their ancestors, God insists that each person is judged by their own choices and pleads with them to turn around and live.

parts.label: The sour grapes saying (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: People had a popular saying: the parents ate sour grapes and the children got the sour taste, meaning they were paying for their ancestors' sins. God rejects it, saying every life belongs to him and the one who sins is the one who will die.

parts.label: A good man (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: The list targets common wrongs of that time, like feasting at hilltop shrines to idols and keeping a poor borrower's pledged cloak overnight, which the law forbade. It joins faithfulness to God with fair dealing, refusing to profit from a neighbor's need, and feeding and clothing the poor.

parts.label: His violent son, his grandson (vv. 10-18)
parts.note: A good father cannot shield a violent son, and a bad father does not doom a son who sees his father's ways and chooses differently. Each of the three generations stands or falls on his own life.

parts.label: No shared guilt (vv. 19-20)
parts.note: The people push back, asking why the son should not carry his father's guilt. The answer repeats the core rule: guilt and goodness belong to the person who did them, not to their parents or children.

parts.label: Turning around changes things (vv. 21-29)
parts.note: A wicked person who truly turns from wrong will live, with the past not held against them, while a good person who turns to evil cannot lean on past goodness. God says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and when the people call this unfair, he says it is their ways that are unfair.

parts.label: Repent and live (vv. 30-32)
parts.note: The chapter ends with an urgent appeal to turn from wrongdoing and get a new heart and spirit, meaning a new inner life and direction, because God takes no pleasure in anyone's death. Later in the book God promises to give that new heart himself (36:26), and Christians often read the two passages together.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether 'live' and 'die' here mean surviving or perishing in the national disaster of that time or something larger, like eternal life and death, which shapes how directly the chapter is applied to salvation today.
think: How much should a person be held responsible for their own choices, when so much of who they become is shaped by the family and the times they were born into?
